query: Earlier studies established BCC refractory high-entropy alloys such as MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW with excellent high-temperature mechanical properties, while systems including AlNbTiV, NbHfTiV, and AlCrNbTiV also showed favorable mechanical behavior. NbZrTi-based alloys provide broad scope for regulating composition and properties, but changes in elemental identity and proportion can alter both phase constitution and mechanical performance. Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC solid solution with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa; however, its high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity. Given the constraint of preserving high strength while improving plasticity under room-temperature compression, what single intervention could overcome this limitation? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and its mechanism, predicts quantitative or directional changes relative to equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo, defines the conditions and limits of the effect, cites supporting evidence from the prior results summarized above, and proposes an experiment with explicit observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partially replacing Mo with additional Nb in equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo will lower the effective electronegativity difference and reduce local bond heterogeneity, thereby enhancing dislocation mobility and room‐temperature ductility while largely preserving high compressive yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy that forms a disordered BCC solid solution with high Mo content; its strong Mo-related bonding elevates strength but limits plastic deformation.
generation.intervention: Reduce the Mo content by substituting roughly 20 atomic percent of Mo with additional Nb (i.e. adjusting the composition to Nb-rich in place of some Mo) to moderate the bond strength heterogeneity.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature compression conditions on alloys processed using conventional casting/HIP and appropriate heat treatments that yield a uniform BCC phase.
generation.structural_mediator: A modified lattice with reduced local lattice distortion and less pronounced electronegativity differences, which facilitates dislocation glide without compromising substantial solid-solution strengthening.
generation.mechanism: The key mechanism is that high Mo content creates strong, less mobile bonds due to large electronegativity differences. By replacing part of Mo with Nb—which has a lower electronegativity and is known to enhance ductility in refractory HEAs—the lattice friction is reduced. This improves the mobility of edge dislocations during compression, resulting in enhanced plasticity while keeping sufficient hardening from the refractory ensemble.
generation.predicted_outcome: A notable increase in room-temperature compressive plastic strain (e.g., achieving plastic strains above 10%) with the yield strength remaining within roughly 10% of the original 1719 MPa value.
generation.baseline: The original equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy, characterized by high yield strength (~1719 MPa) but limited ductility due to the high Mo content.
generation.boundary: This effect is anticipated only if the Mo reduction is moderate (e.g., about 20 at%) since overly reducing Mo may erode the necessary solid-solution strengthening. The enhancement is specific to room-temperature compression in alloys that can maintain a stable single-phase BCC structure.
generation.uncertainty: The proposal combines insights from studies showing that increased Nb content improves ductility in related refractory HEAs (e.g., evidence from PMC7514121 and PMC5995863) with the known effect of Mo’s strong bonding (leading to limited plasticity) in NbZrTiHfMo. The precise quantitative balance between retained strength and improved ductility in this system is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of alloys based on NbZrTiHfMo where Mo is systematically reduced and replaced with extra Nb (for example, series with 100%, 80%, and 60% of the original Mo content, with Nb adjusted accordingly). Process these samples identically and perform room-temperature compression tests.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (via XRD and TEM) to verify phase stability and dislocation characteristics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with reduced Mo do not exhibit a significant improvement in compressive ductility (i.e. achieving >10% strain) while maintaining a yield strength within ~10% of 1719 MPa, or if deleterious phases emerge that undermine the alloy’s uniform BCC structure, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The main goal of the present work was to improve the room temperature ductility of an initially brittle RHEA through microstructure modifications by thermal treatment. The goal was successfully achieved and an improved balance of high strength and good compressive ductility was demonstrated by “inverting” the microstructure from a continuous B2 matrix with discrete BCC precipitates to one consisting of a continuous BCC matrix with discrete B2 precipitates. The details of the strengthening mechanisms in these microstructures are beyond of the scope of the present study. However, it can be speculated that strong element bonding in the B2 matrix is responsible for high strength (and, unfortunately, brittleness) of Condition (1); while in the case of Conditions (2) and (3), precipitation strengthening from B2 precipitates and dislocation mobility in BCC matrix are likely to play a substantial role. Comparing the performance at room temperature, HfMoTaTiZr alloy has the best yield strength 1600 MPa; HfMoNbTaTi has the highest 27% fracture strain; comprehensively, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical properties (yield strength 1369 MPa and 27% fracture strain). The fracture strain increases from 4% for the HfMoTaTiZr alloy to 12% for HfMoNbTaTiZr. The presence of Ta can increase the yield strength but decrease the toughness. Ti seems to have no significant influence on strength, but it has a negative effect on toughness. Zr increases the strength; however, it strongly deteriorates the toughness at room temperature, because the fracture strain decreases from 27% for the HfMoNbTaTi alloy to 12% for HfMoNbTaTiZr. The presence of Mo, which has the highest shear modulus, increases the yield strength at room temperature from 929 MPa to 1512 MPa significantly. Nevertheless, the toughness decreases tremendously, fracture strain declines from > 50% to 12%.
